n: Balaam finally understands that the Lord wants to bless Israel. He stops seeking omens and simply looks toward Israel’s camp in the wilderness.

f.g: Omens or sorcery — the methods of pagan divination Balaam had used before.

n: He sees Israel camped by tribes in God’s appointed order, and the Spirit of God comes upon him. Even an imperfect man can be moved by God’s Spirit for His purposes.

f.w: the spirit of God came upon him

n: Balaam’s third oracle opens by describing himself as a man whose eyes have been opened — fitting, since the angel had to open his eyes on the road.

f.w: the man whose eyes are open

n: He has heard God’s words and seen a vision of the Almighty, falling down yet seeing clearly.

f.g: Hebrew Shaddai — an ancient name for God, as in El Shaddai (Genesis 17:1).
Not in the Hebrew; literally “falling down,” perhaps prostrate before God.

n: “How beautiful are your tents, O Jacob!” These words are still sung in Jewish synagogues as worship begins (the Ma Tovu).

f.g: goodly = beautiful, fine

n: Israel is pictured as lush gardens and trees beside water — a vision of a well-watered, flourishing people in a dry land, like Eden.

f.g: Aloe-wood trees, prized for their fragrance.

f.w: as gardens by the river's side

n: Overflowing water means abundance; Israel’s descendants will spread far. Israel’s king will be greater than Agag, a name used by Amalekite kings.

f.w: his seed shall be in many waters
f.g: His descendants will be many and well-provided — water symbolizing life and prosperity.

n: Repeating the second oracle’s image, Israel has the strength of a wild ox to overcome its enemies.

f.g: The wild ox, not a mythical creature.

n: Like a resting lion no one dares disturb, Israel is secure. Balaam ends with the promise God gave Abraham: those who bless Israel are blessed, and those who curse it are cursed — ironically, a warning to Balak himself.

f.g: couched = crouched, lay down

f.w: Blessed is he that blesseth thee

n: Furious, Balak claps his hands in anger — he has paid for three curses and received three blessings.

f.g: A gesture of anger and scorn.

n: Balak orders Balaam home without reward, sarcastically blaming the Lord for keeping Balaam from honor.

f.g: “Get out — go home!”

n: Balaam reminds Balak of what he told the messengers from the start.
Even for a houseful of silver and gold, he could not do anything — good or bad — on his own; he must speak what the Lord says.

f.g: By my own choice or initiative.

n: Before leaving, Balaam offers one more prophecy, unasked: what Israel will do to Moab in the latter days.

f.g: advertise = inform, advise
Hebrew “the end of days” — the distant future.

n: His fourth oracle begins with the same solemn introduction.
He adds that he knew the knowledge of the Most High — a title for God as supreme over all.

f.g: Hebrew Elyon, a title for God (Genesis 14:18-20).

n: A famous messianic prophecy: a Star and a Sceptre (a king’s rod) will rise from Israel. It was first fulfilled in King David, who conquered Moab; Christians see its fullest meaning in Jesus Christ, the royal Son of David whose birth was announced by a star.

f.w: there shall come a Star out of Jacob

f.g: Possibly a name for a tribal group in Moab; some read it as “sons of tumult.”

n: Edom and Seir (its mountain country) will be conquered, while Israel triumphs. This came true under David.

f.g: The mountainous region of Edom, south of the Dead Sea.

n: A ruler from Jacob will have dominion and destroy his enemies’ remnant.

f.g: Rule, authority.

n: Looking toward Amalek, Israel’s first attacker after the Exodus, Balaam foretells its eventual destruction.

f.w: Amalek was the first of the nations

n: He looks next at the Kenites, a people living in rocky strongholds. “Nest” (qen) is a wordplay on their name.

f.g: A clan related to Moses’ father-in-law (Judges 1:16).

n: Yet even the Kenites will be carried away when Assyria (Asshur) comes — a prophecy of the great empire that would one day dominate the region.

f.g: Assyria, the Mesopotamian empire that rose centuries later.

n: Balaam cries out: who can survive when God carries out these judgments?
Ships from Chittim (Cyprus, or more broadly the western sea peoples) will afflict Assyria and Eber, but they too will perish. Every empire rises and falls under God’s hand.

f.g: Kittim — originally Cyprus, later used for western sea powers such as Greece or Rome (Daniel 11:30).
Possibly peoples east of the Euphrates, or the Hebrews’ ancestral line (Genesis 10:21).

n: Balaam returns home and Balak goes his way. But the story isn’t over: Balaam’s advice will soon lead Israel into sin at Peor.
